title: OOP: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism
problem: Any class can reach into any other class's fields, so the overdraft check is copied into three places, and every new vehicle type means hunting down every switch on type.
summary: The four OOP pillars: encapsulation keeps invariants behind methods, abstraction hides how behind an interface, inheritance models is-a at a cost, and polymorphism replaces conditionals on type with calls that dispatch on the object's class.
catTip: I am an instance of Cat. My hunger is a private field, reachable only through feed(), which validates nothing and accepts every call. Perfectly encapsulated; the invariant is simply 'more'.

recall.q: A `Cart` exposes its item list as a public field and three services add to it directly. Which pillar is broken, what is the concrete risk, and what is the fix?
recall.a: Encapsulation: nothing enforces the cart's invariants (quantity above zero, total matching the lines), so any caller can corrupt it. Make the list private and expose `addItem` and `removeItem`, which validate and keep the total consistent.

guide.breaks: Without encapsulation and abstraction every rule is enforced at the call site, so a negative balance or a vendor-specific exception leaks into the whole codebase and each new type adds another branch to every switch.
guide.tradeoffs: Hiding state and dispatching through interfaces adds indirection: an operation spread across many classes is harder to read than one switch, and an interface for a single implementation is ceremony.
guide.explainSimply: Think of a vending machine. You press a button and a drink appears; you cannot reach into the coin box, and you do not know whether a spiral or a belt moved the can. Objects work the same way: they hide their insides and promise only what their buttons do.
guide.hint: Which pillar is about who may change an object's state, and what single sentence should the fix guarantee?

meow: Private fur, public purr. You may call pet(); you may not set mood directly. Meow-thods only.

quiz.prompt: A `Cart` class exposes `public List<Item> items`, and other classes add to it directly. Which pillar is broken, and what is the concrete harm?
options: Abstraction, because callers can see that the field is a List rather than a Set
Encapsulation, because nothing enforces the cart's invariants, such as a positive quantity or a total that matches the items
Polymorphism, because List is an interface and callers should depend on ArrayList
Inheritance, because Cart should extend ArrayList to expose items safely
quiz.explanation: Encapsulation means the class's methods are the only path to its state, so each one can keep the invariants true. Seeing the collection type is at most a minor abstraction leak; the real harm is that any caller can corrupt the cart.

quiz.prompt: You replace `switch (vehicle.type())` in a fee calculator with a polymorphic `vehicle.hourlyFee()` call. What is the main benefit?
options: Virtual dispatch is significantly faster than a switch statement
Adding a new vehicle type no longer requires editing the calculator or any other caller
The code no longer needs an interface or an abstract class
It makes the set of vehicle types closed, so the compiler reports missing cases
quiz.explanation: Polymorphism moves each case into the class that knows the answer, so a new type is a new class and existing callers stay untouched. Dispatch speed is not the point and is often no better than a switch; a closed set with compiler checks is what a sealed type plus a switch gives you, which is the opposite trade-off.

cards.q: Why is 'a getter and a setter for every field' not encapsulation?
cards.a: Because any caller can still put the object into an invalid state (`setBalance(-1)`). Encapsulation means the class's methods are the only path to its state and each method preserves the invariants, so the check lives in one place.

cards.q: The same `switch (shape.type())` appears in three methods. What does polymorphism do to the three switches, and when would you keep the switch?
cards.a: Each case moves into the shape's class as a method, so a new shape touches no caller. Keep the switch when the set of types is closed and the operations change often: one operation stays in one place, and a `switch` over a `sealed` interface is checked for missing cases.

glossary.note: Organising code as objects that hide state behind methods; its four pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.
